claim: The sympathetic nervous system (SNS) mediates bone metabolism.
source: There is clear evidence that the sympathetic nervous system (SNS) mediates bone metabolism.
evidence: This is stated as clear evidence in the abstract, supported by the subsequent histological and experimental findings described in the manuscript.

claim: Histological studies show abundant SNS innervation of the periosteum and bone marrow.
source: Histological studies show abundant SNS innervation of the periosteum and bone marrow–these nerves consist of noradrenergic fibers that immunostain for tyrosine hydroxylase, dopamine beta-hydroxylase, or neuropeptide Y.
evidence: This claim references histological studies and is supported by citations to prior work (Francis et al., 1997; Hill and Elde, 1991; Hohmann et al., 1986; Martin et al., 2007) mentioned later in the manuscript.

claim: SNS nerves in bone consist of noradrenergic fibers that immunostain for tyrosine hydroxylase, dopamine beta-hydroxylase, or neuropeptide Y.
source: Histological studies show abundant SNS innervation of the periosteum and bone marrow–these nerves consist of noradrenergic fibers that immunostain for tyrosine hydroxylase, dopamine beta-hydroxylase, or neuropeptide Y.
evidence: This is supported by citations to histological studies (Francis et al., 1997; Hill and Elde, 1991; Hohmann et al., 1986; Martin et al., 2007).

claim: The brain sites that send efferent SNS outflow to bone have not yet been characterized prior to this study.
source: Nonetheless, the brain sites that send efferent SNS outflow to the bone have not yet been characterized.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: The central SNS outflow to bone originates from 87 brain nuclei, sub-nuclei, and regions of six brain divisions.
source: We find that the central SNS outflow to bone originates from 87 brain nuclei, sub-nuclei, and regions of six brain divisions, namely the midbrain and pons, hypothalamus, hindbrain medulla, forebrain, cerebral cortex, and thalamus.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on PRV152 viral tracing data presented in Figure 2.

claim: The six brain divisions that send SNS outflow to bone are the midbrain and pons, hypothalamus, hindbrain medulla, forebrain, cerebral cortex, and thalamus.
source: We find that the central SNS outflow to bone originates from 87 brain nuclei, sub-nuclei, and regions of six brain divisions, namely the midbrain and pons, hypothalamus, hindbrain medulla, forebrain, cerebral cortex, and thalamus.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on the viral tracing experiments.

claim: The raphe magnus (RMg) of the medulla displays greater degrees of PRV152 infection.
source: We also find that certain sites, such as the raphe magnus (RMg) of the medulla and periaqueductal gray (PAG) of the midbrain, display greater degrees of PRV152 infection, suggesting that there is considerable site-specific variation in the levels of central SNS outflow to the bone.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of PRV152-infected neurons shown in Figure 2.

claim: The periaqueductal gray (PAG) of the midbrain displays greater degrees of PRV152 infection.
source: We also find that certain sites, such as the raphe magnus (RMg) of the medulla and periaqueductal gray (PAG) of the midbrain, display greater degrees of PRV152 infection, suggesting that there is considerable site-specific variation in the levels of central SNS outflow to the bone.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of PRV152-infected neurons shown in Figure 2.

claim: There is considerable site-specific variation in the levels of central SNS outflow to bone.
source: We also find that certain sites, such as the raphe magnus (RMg) of the medulla and periaqueductal gray (PAG) of the midbrain, display greater degrees of PRV152 infection, suggesting that there is considerable site-specific variation in the levels of central SNS outflow to the bone.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential levels of PRV152 infection across brain regions.

claim: Increased SNS tone causes bone loss through a reduction in bone formation coupled with increased bone resorption.
source: Elegant studies have suggested that increased SNS tone causes bone loss through a reduction in bone formation, which is coupled with increased bone resorption (Elefteriou, 2018; Elefteriou et al., 2005; Takeda et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The anti-osteogenic actions of leptin are mediated centrally by glucose-responsive neurons in the ventromedial hypothalamus through peripheral SNS pathways.
source: It has also been shown using leptin-deficient mice with a high bone mass that the anti-osteogenic actions of leptin are mediated centrally by glucose-responsive neurons in the ventromedial hypothalamus through peripheral SNS pathways (Ducy et al., 2000; Takeda et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies using leptin-deficient mice.

claim: Both the periosteum and bone marrow are innervated richly by the SNS as evidenced by immunoreactive tyrosine hydroxylase, dopamine beta-hydroxylase, or neuropeptide Y fibers.
source: Furthermore, both the periosteum and the bone marrow are innervated richly by the SNS as evidenced by immunoreactive tyrosine hydroxylase, dopamine beta-hydroxylase, or neuropeptide Y fibers.
evidence: This is supported by citations to immunohistochemical studies (Francis et al., 1997; Hill and Elde, 1991; Hohmann et al., 1986; Martin et al., 2007).

claim: SNS markers are associated mostly with the vasculature and SNS vesicular acetylcholine transporter (VAChT).
source: These latter SNS markers are associated mostly with the vasculature and SNS vesicular acetylcholine transporter (VAChT), whereas vasoactive intestinal polypeptide (VIP) immunoreactive fibers display mainly a parenchymal location (Francis et al., 1997; Hill and Elde, 1991; Hohmann et al., 1986; Martin et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior immunohistochemical studies.

claim: Vasoactive intestinal polypeptide (VIP) immunoreactive fibers display mainly a parenchymal location.
source: These latter SNS markers are associated mostly with the vasculature and SNS vesicular acetylcholine transporter (VAChT), whereas vasoactive intestinal polypeptide (VIP) immunoreactive fibers display mainly a parenchymal location (Francis et al., 1997; Hill and Elde, 1991; Hohmann et al., 1986; Martin et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior immunohistochemical studies.

claim: The distribution of SNS nerves within the mammalian skeleton and their connectivity to central neurons is far from being completely understood.
source: Despite these studies, the distribution of SNS nerves within the mammalian skeleton and their connectivity to central neurons is far from being completely understood.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap that motivates the current study.

claim: Bartha's K strain of PRV is a transneuronal tract tracer that provides the ability to map multi-synaptic circuits within the same animal.
source: Bartha's K strain of the PRV is a transneuronal tract tracer that provides the ability to map multi-synaptic circuits within the same animal (Ekstrand et al., 2008; Enquist, 2002; Song et al., 2005a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior methodological studies.

claim: PRVs are transported exclusively in a retrograde manner from the dendrites of infected neurons to axons.
source: Transported exclusively in a retrograde manner from the dendrites of the infected neurons to axons, PRVs first make synaptic contact with neuronal cell bodies, and undergo self-amplification and thereafter continue their specific backward ascent (Curanovic and Enquist, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work on PRV transport mechanisms.

claim: PRV infection progresses along the neuroaxis chain from the periphery to higher CNS sites.
source: This results in an infection that progresses along the neuroaxis chain from the periphery to higher CNS sites (Ekstrand et al., 2008; Enquist, 2002; Song et al., 2005a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies on PRV tracing.

claim: Postganglionic SNS innervation of specific white and brown adipose tissue depots has separate and shared central SNS relay sites.
source: Utilizing this viral technology, we have previously shown postganglionic SNS innervation of specific white and brown adipose tissue depots with the separate and shared central SNS relay sites (Ryu and Bartness, 2014; Ryu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the authors' prior work.

claim: There is a direct neuroanatomical connection between phosphodiesterase 5 A (PDE5A)-containing neurons in specific brain nuclei and bone.
source: Moreover, we have established a direct neuroanatomical connection between phosphodiesterase 5 A (PDE5A)-containing neurons in specific brain nuclei and bone, inferring a contribution of the central nodes to the bone-forming actions of PDE5A inhibitors (Kim et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' prior work.

claim: A hierarchical circuit controlling SNS output to rat femoral epiphyseal bone marrow has been defined by identifying PRVs in the ganglia and paravertebral chain in the intermediolateral column (IML) of the lower thoracic spinal cord.
source: A hierarchical circuit controlling SNS output to rat femoral epiphyseal bone marrow has also been defined by identifying PRVs in the ganglia and paravertebral chain in the intermediolateral column (IML) of the lower thoracic spinal cord (Dénes et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Neurons in C1, A5, A7 catecholaminergic cell groups, several other nuclei of the ventrolateral and ventromedial medulla, periaqueductal gray, the paraventricular hypothalamic nucleus, among other hypothalamic nuclei, as well as the insular and piriform cortex comprise the known central network sending SNS outflow to bone marrow.
source: In addition, neurons in C1, A5, A7 catecholaminergic cell groups, several other nuclei of the ventrolateral and ventromedial medulla, periaqueductal gray, the paraventricular hypothalamic nucleus, among other hypothalamic nuclei, as well as the insular and piriform cortex comprise the known central network sending SNS outflow to bone marrow (Dénes et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: No studies have yet mapped the exact localization and organization of the central SNS circuitry innervating the murine femur prior to this study.
source: However, no studies have yet mapped the exact localization and organization of the central SNS circuitry innervating the murine femur.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap that the current study addresses.

claim: Mice remained asymptomatic until day 5 post-inoculation following PRV152 infections.
source: Following PRV152 infections, mice remained asymptomatic until day 5 post-inoculation, after which time, mice began to display symptoms of infection, including occasional loss of body weight and decreased mobility, but most often an ungroomed coat.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental procedures.

claim: After day 5 post-inoculation, mice began to display symptoms of infection including occasional loss of body weight, decreased mobility, and most often an ungroomed coat.
source: Following PRV152 infections, mice remained asymptomatic until day 5 post-inoculation, after which time, mice began to display symptoms of infection, including occasional loss of body weight and decreased mobility, but most often an ungroomed coat.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental procedures.

claim: Four of six mice were equally infected by PRV152 throughout the neuroaxis from the hindbrain to the forebrain.
source: Four of six mice were equally infected by PRV152 throughout the neuroaxis from the hindbrain to the forebrain and therefore were included in the analyses.
evidence: This is a methodological observation about the experimental sample.

claim: Two mice exhibited over-infection by PRV152 as evidenced by widespread cloudy plaques surrounding the infected neurons and were excluded from the analysis.
source: Two mice exhibited over-infection by PRV152, as evidenced by widespread cloudy plaques surrounding the infected neurons; these mice were excluded from the analysis.
evidence: This is a methodological observation about quality control in the experiments.

claim: PRV152-labeled neurons were found in the IML of the spinal cord.
source: We also found PRV152-labeled neurons in the IML of the spinal cord in accordance with our previous studies that defined SNS innervations of fat pads in the Siberian hamster (Ryu and Bartness, 2014; Ryu et al., 2015; Ryu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study supported by prior work.

claim: Unilateral PRV152 microinjection into the right femur appeared bilaterally in the brain with almost unnoticeable domination of the viral infection between the two hemispheres.
source: Unilateral PRV152 microinjection into the right femur appeared bilaterally in the brain with almost unnoticeable domination of the viral infection between the two hemispheres.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental results.

claim: Prior studies on SNS and sensory innervations of various fat depots produced no ipsilateral differences between the innervation patterns of SNS or sensory system with unilateral viral inoculation.
source: Likewise, prior studies on SNS and sensory innervations of various fat depots, utilizing the SNS tract tracer PRV152 and sensory system tract tracer HSV-1 produced no ipsilateral differences between the innervation patterns of SNS or sensory system with unilateral viral inoculation (Bamshad et al., 1999; Leitner and Bartness, 2009; Song et al., 2008; Vaughan and Bartness, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: No EGFP signal was detected in the PVH when PRV152 was placed on the bone surface rather than injected into the periosteum or metaphysis.
source: To validate the retrograde tract tracing methodology, we placed PRV152 at the same titer on the bone surface, rather than injecting it into the periosteum or metaphysis. No EGFP signal was detected in the PVH that is known to possess sympathetic pre-autonomic neurons or in the RPa (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a control experiment shown in Figure 1A demonstrating specificity of the injection method.

claim: PRV152 injections into the periosteum or metaphysis resulted in positive EGFP immunostaining in the PVH.
source: By contrast, PRV152 injections into the periosteum or metaphysis resulted in positive EGFP immunostaining in the PVH (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B as validation of the injection method.

claim: PRV152-infected neurons were found in the IML of the spinal cord at T13-L2 levels.
source: In addition, we found PRV152-infected neurons in the IML of the spinal cord, at T13-L2 levels (Figure 1B), suggesting specific bone-SNS ganglia-IML-brain route of infection; this is consistent with prior findings wherein PRV152 individually infected the classic SNS spinal cord neurons (Bamshad et al., 1999; Ryu and Bartness, 2014; Ryu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The hypothalamus has the most PRV152-infected SNS neurons connecting to bone (1177.25±62.75).
source: We identified 87 PRV152-positive brain nuclei, sub-nuclei, and regions within six brain divisions, with the hypothalamus having the most PRV152-infected SNS neurons connecting to bone (1177.25±62.75), followed, in descending order, by midbrain and pons (1065±22.39), hindbrain medulla (495.25±33.49), forebrain (237.5±15.08), cerebral cortex (104.75±4.64) and thalamus (65.25±7.78) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the study shown in Figure 2.

claim: Midbrain and pons have 1065±22.39 PRV152-infected SNS neurons connecting to bone.
source: We identified 87 PRV152-positive brain nuclei, sub-nuclei, and regions within six brain divisions, with the hypothalamus having the most PRV152-infected SNS neurons connecting to bone (1177.25±62.75), followed, in descending order, by midbrain and pons (1065±22.39), hindbrain medulla (495.25±33.49), forebrain (237.5±15.08), cerebral cortex (104.75±4.64) and thalamus (65.25±7.78) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the study shown in Figure 2.

claim: Hindbrain medulla has 495.25±33.49 PRV152-infected SNS neurons connecting to bone.
source: We identified 87 PRV152-positive brain nuclei, sub-nuclei, and regions within six brain divisions, with the hypothalamus having the most PRV152-infected SNS neurons connecting to bone (1177.25±62.75), followed, in descending order, by midbrain and pons (1065±22.39), hindbrain medulla (495.25±33.49), forebrain (237.5±15.08), cerebral cortex (104.75±4.64) and thalamus (65.25±7.78) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the study shown in Figure 2.

claim: Forebrain has 237.5±15.08 PRV152-infected SNS neurons connecting to bone.
source: We identified 87 PRV152-positive brain nuclei, sub-nuclei, and regions within six brain divisions, with the hypothalamus having the most PRV152-infected SNS neurons connecting to bone (1177.25±62.75), followed, in descending order, by midbrain and pons (1065±22.39), hindbrain medulla (495.25±33.49), forebrain (237.5±15.08), cerebral cortex (104.75±4.64) and thalamus (65.25±7.78) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the study shown in Figure 2.

claim: Cerebral cortex has 104.75±4.64 PRV152-infected SNS neurons connecting to bone.
source: We identified 87 PRV152-positive brain nuclei, sub-nuclei, and regions within six brain divisions, with the hypothalamus having the most PRV152-infected SNS neurons connecting to bone (1177.25±62.75), followed, in descending order, by midbrain and pons (1065±22.39), hindbrain medulla (495.25±33.49), forebrain (237.5±15.08), cerebral cortex (104.75±4.64) and thalamus (65.25±7.78) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the study shown in Figure 2.

claim: Thalamus has 65.25±7.78 PRV152-infected SNS neurons connecting to bone.
source: We identified 87 PRV152-positive brain nuclei, sub-nuclei, and regions within six brain divisions, with the hypothalamus having the most PRV152-infected SNS neurons connecting to bone (1177.25±62.75), followed, in descending order, by midbrain and pons (1065±22.39), hindbrain medulla (495.25±33.49), forebrain (237.5±15.08), cerebral cortex (104.75±4.64) and thalamus (65.25±7.78) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the study shown in Figure 2.

claim: Hypothalamic areas with the highest percentages of PRV152-labeled neurons include the lateral hypothalamus (LH), PVH and dorsomedial hypothalamus (DM).
source: Hypothalamic areas with the highest percentages of PRV152-labeled neurons included the lateral hypothalamus (LH), PVH and dorsomedial hypothalamus (DM) (Figure 1B and Figure 2; see Appendix for a glossary of brain nuclei, sub-nuclei and regions).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis shown in Figures 1B and 2.

claim: The LH and PVH are among the regions with the highest absolute numbers of infected neurons among 25 PRV152-positive nuclei, sub-nuclei, and regions in the hypothalamus.
source: The LH and PVH also were among the regions with the highest absolute numbers of infected neurons of the 25 PRV152-positive nuclei, sub-nuclei, and regions.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: In the midbrain and pons, areas with the highest percentages and counts of PRV152-infected neurons include the PAG, lateral PAG (LPAG) and pontine reticular nucleus, oral part (PnO), among 18 nuclei, sub-nuclei, and regions.
source: In the midbrain and pons, areas with the highest percentages and counts of PRV152-infected neurons included the PAG, lateral PAG (LPAG) and pontine reticular nucleus, oral part (PnO), among 18 nuclei, sub-nuclei, and regions.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: In the hindbrain medulla, the raphe pallidus nucleus (RPa), RMg, and gigantocellular reticular nucleus (Gi) are among 23 nuclei, sub-nuclei and regions heavily represented by the largest percentages and counts of PRV152-labeled neurons.
source: Single-labeled neurons were also notable in the hindbrain medulla, where the raphe pallidus nucleus (RPa), RMg, and gigantocellular reticular nucleus (Gi) were among 23 nuclei, sub-nuclei and regions, heavily represented by the largest percentages and counts of PRV152-labeled neurons.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The forebrain areas with the highest percentages and numbers of PRV152-labeled neurons are the medial preoptic nucleus, medial part (MPOM), bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BST), and lateral septal nucleus, ventral part (LSV) among 15 PRV152-positive nuclei, sub-nuclei, and regions.
source: The forebrain areas with the highest percentages and numbers of PRV152-labeled neurons were the medial preoptic nucleus, medial part (MPOM), bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BST), and lateral septal nucleus, ventral part (LSV) among 15 PRV152-positive nuclei, sub-nuclei, and regions.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: In the cerebral cortex, there are only three regions containing PRV152-labeled neurons: the primary somatosensory cortex, hindlimb region (S1HL), and secondary and primary motor cortex (M2 and M1, respectively).
source: In the cerebral cortex, there were only three regions containing PRV152-labeled neurons–namely, the primary somatosensory cortex, hindlimb region (S1HL), and secondary and primary motor cortex (M2 and M1, respectively).
evidence: This is based on the viral tracing results shown in Figure 2.

claim: The S1HL and M2 had both the highest percentages and numbers of PRV152-labeled neurons in the cerebral cortex.
source: The S1HL and M2 had both the highest percentages and numbers of PRV152-labeled neurons.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Three brain sites with PRV152-infected neurons were detected within the thalamus.
source: Finally, we detected 3 brain sites with PRV152-infected neurons within the thalamus.
evidence: This is based on the viral tracing results shown in Figure 2.

claim: Among the thalamic nuclei possessing the highest percentages and numbers of PRV152-labeled neurons are the periventricular fiber system (pv) and precommisural nucleus (PrC).
source: Among the nuclei possessing the highest percentages and numbers of PRV152-labeled neurons were the periventricular fiber system (pv) and precommisural nucleus (PrC).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: When injected into peripheral tissues, PRV152 travels exclusively in a retrograde manner via synaptically-linked neurons.
source: When injected into peripheral tissues, PRV152 travels exclusively in a retrograde manner via synaptically-linked neurons.
evidence: This is a known property of PRV152 supported by prior literature and used as the basis for the experimental design.

claim: PRV152 first infects SNS postganglionic neurons at L1-L2 levels, followed by infection of SNS preganglionic neurons in the IML of the spinal cord and finally ascending to the brain.
source: First, the virus infects SNS postganglionic neurons at L1-L2 levels, followed by infection of SNS preganglionic neurons in the IML of the spinal cord and, finally, ascending to the brain.
evidence: This describes the progression of viral infection observed in the study.

claim: PRV152 yields a hierarchical chain of functionally connected neurons, allowing the mapping of the entire femur-brain neuroaxis.
source: This yields a hierarchical chain of functionally connected neurons, thus allowing the mapping of the entire femur-brain neuroaxis.
evidence: This is a methodological principle underlying the experimental approach.

claim: The PRV152 neural tract tracer especially predominates in the PAG of the midbrain, LH of the hypothalamus, RPa of the medulla, MPOM of the forebrain, S1HL of the cortex, and pv of the thalamus.
source: Notably, the PRV152 neural tract tracer especially predominates in the PAG of the midbrain, LH of the hypothalamus, RPa of the medulla, MPOM of the forebrain, S1HL of the cortex, and pv of the thalamus.
evidence: This is based on the quantitative analysis of PRV152 infection shown in Figure 2.

claim: The SNS regulates bone remodeling and bone mass in mice.
source: Neuroanatomical and functional evidence in mice suggests that the SNS regulates bone remodeling and bone mass (Ducy et al., 2000; Francis et al., 1997; Hill and Elde, 1991; Hohmann et al., 1986; Martin et al., 2007; Takeda et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Leptin acts as an anti-osteogenesis signal through glucose responsive neurons in the VMH via peripheral SNS relay.
source: Furthermore, it is clear that leptin acts as an anti-osteogenesis signal through glucose responsive neurons in the VMH via peripheral SNS relay (Takeda et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Dopamine-transporter-deficient mice with no rapid uptake of dopamine into presynaptic terminals are osteopenic.
source: Likewise, dopamine-transporter-deficient mice with no rapid uptake of dopamine into presynaptic terminals are osteopenic (Bliziotes et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Multisynaptic tract tracing has identified limited hierarchical central circuitry controlling SNS innervation of rat femoral epiphyseal bone marrow and bone.
source: Multisynaptic tract tracing has identified limited hierarchical central circuitry controlling SNS innervation of rat femoral epiphyseal bone marrow and bone (Dénes et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Several SNS pathways from the brainstem and the hypothalamus relay to femoral bone marrow and the femur through preganglionic neurons in the lower thoracic and upper lumbar segments T4 to L1 of the IML and postganglionic neurons in paravertebral chain ganglia at lumbar levels.
source: Several SNS pathways from the brainstem and the hypothalamus relay to femoral bone marrow and the femur through preganglionic neurons in the lower thoracic and upper lumbar segments T4 to L1 of the IML and postganglionic neurons in paravertebral chain ganglia at lumbar levels (Dénes et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Largely the same brain sites project to both the femur and bone marrow.
source: Despite the fact that largely the same brain sites project to both the femur (our findings) and bone marrow (Dénes et al., 2005), some sites display higher levels of PRV152 infectivity than others–this suggests that separate site-specific SNS circuits may project to the femur and femoral bone marrow.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the current findings with prior work.

claim: Some brain sites display higher levels of PRV152 infectivity than others, suggesting that separate site-specific SNS circuits may project to the femur and femoral bone marrow.
source: Despite the fact that largely the same brain sites project to both the femur (our findings) and bone marrow (Dénes et al., 2005), some sites display higher levels of PRV152 infectivity than others–this suggests that separate site-specific SNS circuits may project to the femur and femoral bone marrow.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential levels of PRV152 infection across brain regions.

claim: Overlapping SNS-innervating circuits to both femur and bone marrow include the midbrain PAG, somatosensory cortex, forebrain MPOM, thalamic periventricular nucleus, hypothalamic PVH, lateral hypothalamic nucleus (LA), and medullary RPa.
source: These overlapping SNS-innervating circuits to both sites include the midbrain PAG, somatosensory cortex, forebrain MPOM, thalamic periventricular nucleus, hypothalamic PVH, lateral hypothalamic nucleus (LA), and medullary RPa.
evidence: This is based on comparing the current findings with prior work on bone marrow.

claim: The PAG receives afferent fibers from the parabrachial nucleus and RPa.
source: The PAG receives afferent fibers not only from the parabrachial nucleus and RPa (Mantyh, 1982), which contain PDE5A-expressing neurons sending SNS outputs to bone (Kim et al., 2020), but also from the spinal cord (Pechura and Liu, 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior anatomical studies.

claim: The parabrachial nucleus and RPa contain PDE5A-expressing neurons sending SNS outputs to bone.
source: The PAG receives afferent fibers not only from the parabrachial nucleus and RPa (Mantyh, 1982), which contain PDE5A-expressing neurons sending SNS outputs to bone (Kim et al., 2020), but also from the spinal cord (Pechura and Liu, 1986).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' prior work.

claim: The PAG receives afferent fibers from the spinal cord.
source: The PAG receives afferent fibers not only from the parabrachial nucleus and RPa (Mantyh, 1982), which contain PDE5A-expressing neurons sending SNS outputs to bone (Kim et al., 2020), but also from the spinal cord (Pechura and Liu, 1986).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior anatomical work.

claim: The PAG sends SNS outflow to WAT in Siberian hamsters.
source: We and others have previously shown that the PAG sends SNS outflow to WAT in Siberian hamsters (Bamshad et al., 1998; Nguyen et al., 2014; Ryu and Bartness, 2014; Song et al., 2005b) and the laboratory rat (Adler et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The PAG sends SNS outflow to WAT in the laboratory rat.
source: We and others have previously shown that the PAG sends SNS outflow to WAT in Siberian hamsters (Bamshad et al., 1998; Nguyen et al., 2014; Ryu and Bartness, 2014; Song et al., 2005b) and the laboratory rat (Adler et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The PAG is largely responsible for SNS responses and descending modulation of pain perception.
source: Most notably, the PAG is largely responsible for SNS responses and descending modulation of pain perception (Baptista-de-Souza et al., 2018; Benarroch, 2008; Calvino and Grilo, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies on PAG function.

claim: The PAG could receive sensory inflow relating to bone pain and provide SNS relay.
source: Therefore, this midbrain node could receive sensory inflow relating to bone pain and provide SNS relay (Figure 3).
evidence: This is inferred from the known functions of PAG and its connectivity to bone shown in the current study.

claim: Nerves that innervate skeletal tissues function in both skeletal pain and anabolism, affecting a variety of skeletal cell types.
source: Furthermore, nerves that innervate skeletal tissues seem to function in both skeletal pain and anabolism, affecting a variety of skeletal cell types.
evidence: This is inferred from the anatomical and functional evidence presented.

claim: Manipulating the SNS or sensory neurons with drug therapies targeted to bone could have effects on bone pain.
source: Identification of SNS neural nodes that regulate skeletal metabolism and nociceptive functions implies that manipulating the SNS or sensory neurons with drug therapies targeted to bone could have effects on bone pain and vice versa.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the findings.

claim: Two major nuclei in the hypothalamus–the PVH and LH–send SNS efferents to the bone.
source: We also find that two major nuclei in the hypothalamus–the PVH and LH–send SNS efferents to the bone.
evidence: This is based on the viral tracing results.

claim: The PVH sends SNS projections to the bone marrow.
source: While the PVH, which is a home to major SNS pre-autonomic neurons, sends SNS projections to the bone marrow (Dénes et al., 2005), we find that LH predominantly innervates the femur.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: LH predominantly innervates the femur.
source: While the PVH, which is a home to major SNS pre-autonomic neurons, sends SNS projections to the bone marrow (Dénes et al., 2005), we find that LH predominantly innervates the femur.
evidence: This is based on the viral tracing results showing high levels of PRV152 infection in LH.

claim: The LH, PVH, and DM are the main brain regions that send SNS outflow to bone and also express leptin receptors.
source: However, given that the LH, PVH, and DM are the main brain regions that send SNS outflow to bone and also express leptin receptors (Flak and Myers, 2016), it is also possible that the anti-osteogenic relay for leptin might originate from neurons in the LH PVH, and/or DM.
evidence: This combines the current findings with prior knowledge about leptin receptor expression.

claim: The anti-osteogenic relay for leptin might originate from neurons in the LH, PVH, and/or DM.
source: However, given that the LH, PVH, and DM are the main brain regions that send SNS outflow to bone and also express leptin receptors (Flak and Myers, 2016), it is also possible that the anti-osteogenic relay for leptin might originate from neurons in the LH PVH, and/or DM.
